concepts.hook: You spilled coffee on your shirt before a meeting. How many people noticed?
concepts.sticker: Quiz: A about half / B about a quarter / C nearly everyone (answer B)
concepts.question: What's the last thing you were sure everyone noticed?
concepts.follow_up: Answer card: students made to wear an embarrassing T-shirt guessed about half the room noticed. About a quarter did. Moodius: the spotlight is mostly in your head, which is good news and mildly insulting.
concepts.cta: Send this to the friend who still talks about the thing from 2019.
concepts.source: Gilovich, Medvec & Savitsky, J. Personality and Social Psychology 78(2), 2000

concepts.hook: You just met someone new and chatted for five minutes. Did they like you more or less than you think?
concepts.sticker: Poll: More than I think / Less than I think
concepts.question: Who did you misjudge on a first meeting?
concepts.follow_up: Researchers call it the liking gap: after first conversations, people kept underestimating how much the other person liked them. Moodius: you're probably more liked than your 1am brain allows.
concepts.cta: Send this to someone who replays every conversation.
concepts.source: Boothby, Clark, Corcoran & Bargh, Psychological Science 29(11), 2018

concepts.hook: You think a compliment will feel awkward. The other person thinks...?
concepts.sticker: Slider 😬 → 😊: how good does a stranger feel after a sincere compliment?
concepts.question: Who deserves a compliment you haven't said out loud?
concepts.follow_up: People giving compliments underestimated how good they made others feel and overestimated how awkward it would be. Moodius: the awkwardness is a toll you pay once.
concepts.cta: Send one compliment today. Reply 'sent' if you did.
concepts.source: Boothby & Bohns, Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin 47(5), 2021

concepts.hook: Talk to the stranger on the train, or keep your headphones in?
concepts.sticker: Poll: Talk / Headphones
concepts.question: When did a conversation with a stranger surprise you?
concepts.follow_up: Commuters asked to talk to a stranger reported a more pleasant journey than those told to keep to themselves, though most predicted the opposite. Moodius: nobody is asking you to befriend the whole carriage. One sentence.
concepts.source: Epley & Schroeder, J. Experimental Psychology: General 143(5), 2014

concepts.hook: Ordering coffee: efficient, or one real sentence with the barista?
concepts.sticker: Poll: Efficient / One real sentence
concepts.question: Who's the small-talk regular in your week?
concepts.follow_up: People told to have a genuine exchange with a barista left in a better mood and felt more connected than people told to be efficient. Moodius: the cheapest wellbeing upgrade in the building.
concepts.cta: Send this to your coffee person.
concepts.source: Sandstrom & Dunn, Social Psychological and Personality Science 5(4), 2014

concepts.hook: You write a thank-you note. How happy will they be, really?
concepts.sticker: Quiz: A a bit / B as much as I'd guess / C more than I'd guess (answer C)
concepts.question: Who has done more for you than you've told them?
concepts.follow_up: Writers of gratitude letters underestimated how surprised and happy recipients felt, and overestimated how awkward they'd feel. Moodius: the note you keep not writing is worth more than you think.
concepts.cta: Reply with one name. That's the note.

concepts.hook: Angry. Hurt. Fine. How many words do you actually use for feelings?
concepts.sticker: Slider 🫥 → 🎨: how precisely can you name what you feel?
concepts.reply_fallback: Reply with today's feeling in one word. 'Fine' not allowed.
concepts.question: What's a feeling you've never had a word for?
concepts.follow_up: People who tell their emotions apart in fine detail tend to cope better under stress. Psychologists call it emotional granularity. Moodius: 'annoyed, slightly jealous, mostly tired' is a better sentence than 'fine'.
concepts.source: Kashdan, Barrett & McKnight, Current Directions in Psychological Science 24(1), 2015

concepts.hook: Saying 'I'm angry' out loud. Does it make it worse or better?
concepts.sticker: Quiz: A worse / B better / C no difference (answer B, in the lab)
concepts.question: What's the feeling you avoid naming?
concepts.follow_up: In a brain-scan study, putting a feeling into words lowered the amygdala's response compared with other tasks. Name it to tame it, roughly. Small lab study, not a cure.

concepts.hook: Before something scary: 'calm down' or 'I'm excited'?
concepts.sticker: Poll: Calm down / I'm excited
concepts.question: What's the scary thing on your calendar?
concepts.follow_up: People told to say 'I am excited' before singing or speaking did better than those told to say 'I am calm'. Same racing heart, different label. Moodius: you can't always calm down. You can rename.
concepts.cta: Send this to someone with a big day this week.

concepts.hook: Marcus Aurelius wrote to himself as 'you'. Weird habit, or smart?
concepts.sticker: Quiz: A just his style / B it helps / C nobody knows (answer B, plausibly)
concepts.question: What would you say to yourself if you were your own friend?
concepts.follow_up: Talking to yourself by name or as 'you' before a stressful task lowered anxiety in experiments. Psychologists call it self-distancing. Marcus was doing it 1,800 years early.
concepts.source: Kross et al., J. Personality and Social Psychology 106(2), 2014; Meditations is addressed to himself

concepts.hook: Right now, honestly: are you here, or somewhere else?
concepts.sticker: Slider 🌫️ → 📍: how present have you been today?
concepts.question: Where does your mind go when it wanders?
concepts.follow_up: A phone study pinged people through the day: minds were wandering in about 47% of samples, and people were less happy when they wandered. Moodius: reading this counts as being here. Well done.

concepts.hook: 15 minutes alone with your thoughts, no phone. Or a mild electric shock?
concepts.sticker: Poll: 15 minutes of thinking / The shock, obviously
concepts.question: When were you last bored on purpose?
concepts.follow_up: In one experiment, many participants chose to give themselves a mild shock rather than sit with their thoughts for 15 minutes. Moodius: the Stoics would have assigned this as homework.
concepts.cta: Send this to the friend who can't wait in a queue without their phone.

concepts.hook: What kept people alive longer across 148 studies?
concepts.sticker: Quiz: A strong relationships / B a strict diet / C a big income (answer A, of these three)
concepts.question: Who's in your 3am contacts?
concepts.follow_up: A review of 148 studies found people with stronger social relationships had about 50% higher odds of survival over the study periods. The authors compared the size to well-known risks like smoking. Linked, not proof of cause.
concepts.cta: Send this to someone you haven't called in a while. No reason needed.

concepts.hook: Your friend says 'look at that bird'. You... ?
concepts.sticker: Poll: Look at the bird / Keep scrolling
concepts.question: What small 'look at this' do you remember someone turning toward?
concepts.follow_up: John Gottman calls these 'bids'. In his lab's newlywed study, couples still together six years later had turned toward bids 86% of the time; couples who divorced, 33%. Reported by the Gottman Institute, not in a journal paper. Moodius: look at the bird.
concepts.cta: Send this to the person who always shows you birds.
concepts.source: The Gottman Institute, 'Turn Toward Instead of Away' (blog); Gottman & DeClaire, The Relationship Cure, 2001

concepts.hook: Two minutes of standing like a superhero changes your hormones.
concepts.sticker: Quiz: Real / Myth / Half true (answer Half true)
concepts.question: What self-help 'fact' did you believe for years?
concepts.follow_up: The 2010 study said yes. A bigger 2015 replication found no hormone change; people did feel more powerful. Moodius: stand however you like. Feeling braver is still something.
concepts.source: Carney, Cuddy & Yap, Psychological Science 2010; Ranehill et al., Psychological Science 26(5), 2015

concepts.hook: A new habit takes 21 days.
concepts.sticker: Quiz: A 21 days / B about 66 days / C 254 days (answer B, median)
concepts.question: What habit are you on day 'some' of?
concepts.follow_up: In a study of people building daily habits, the median time to automatic was 66 days, from 18 to 254. Moodius: if it's day 22 and it still feels like work, you're not broken, you're average.
concepts.cta: Send this to someone on day 22.
concepts.source: Lally et al., European J. Social Psychology 40(6), 2010

concepts.hook: 10,000 hours of practice makes anyone an expert.
concepts.sticker: Quiz: Real / Myth / Half true (answer Half true)
concepts.question: What are you practising that nobody sees?
concepts.follow_up: A big review found deliberate practice explained about 12% of the differences in performance overall, more in games and music, less in professions. Practice matters. It isn't the whole story.

concepts.hook: The marshmallow test predicted kids' futures.
concepts.sticker: Quiz: Real / Myth / Half true (answer Half true)
concepts.question: What were you 'bad at' as a kid that changed?
concepts.follow_up: A larger 2018 replication found the link to later achievement was about half the original size, and much smaller once family background was counted. Moodius: you were not decided by a marshmallow.
concepts.cta: Send this to someone who still feels like the kid who ate it.

concepts.hook: Reading literary fiction makes you better at reading people.
concepts.sticker: Quiz: Real / Myth / Unclear (answer Unclear)
concepts.question: Which book made you understand someone better?
concepts.follow_up: A 2013 Science paper said a short read did it. A large 2016 replication didn't find the effect. Long-term readers may still differ. Moodius: one chapter won't fix you. A lifetime of them might help.
concepts.source: Kidd & Castano, Science 2013; Panero et al., J. Personality and Social Psychology 111(5), 2016

concepts.hook: Your last walk. What did it do to your mood?
concepts.sticker: Slider 🌧️ → ☀️
concepts.question: Where do you walk when you need to think?
concepts.follow_up: A 2024 review of randomised trials found walking or jogging, yoga and strength training all reduced depression, walking among the strongest. Alongside treatment, never instead of it.
concepts.cta: Send this to your walking person.

concepts.hook: How many minutes outside this week? Real outside, not the car park.
concepts.sticker: Slider 🏢 → 🌳 (0 to 3 hours)
concepts.reply_fallback: Reply with your guess in minutes.
concepts.question: Where's the nearest green thing you could sit by?
concepts.follow_up: In a survey of about 20,000 people in England, those who spent at least 120 minutes a week in nature were more likely to report good health and wellbeing. Linked, not proven to cause it.

concepts.hook: Older adults took a 15-minute 'awe walk' each week. What changed in their photos?
concepts.sticker: Quiz: A more selfies / B they got smaller in the frame / C nothing (answer B)
concepts.question: What's the last thing that made you feel small, in a good way?
concepts.follow_up: Over 8 weeks, awe walkers reported more joy and more warm feelings toward others, and their selfies shrank: more sky, less self. Moodius: let the world take up more of the picture.
concepts.cta: Send this to someone who needs a walk with no podcast.

concepts.hook: What does your body do before your mind admits you're stressed?
concepts.sticker: Question box: 'Mine's the jaw. Yours?'
concepts.question: What's your early warning sign?
concepts.follow_up: Moodius take: mine's the shoulders, up near my ears by 4pm. Seneca advised stopping anger at its first signs, before it takes over (On Anger, Book I, paraphrase). Your body is the first sign.
concepts.source: Moodius paraphrase of Seneca, On Anger, Book I

concepts.hook: Honest sleep check. How rested are you right now?
concepts.sticker: Slider 🧟 → 🐣
concepts.question: What's the last thing you do before sleep?
concepts.follow_up: Sleep experts' consensus: adults should regularly get 7 or more hours. Moodius: this story will still be here tomorrow. Go to bed.

concepts.hook: Who do you envy? Don't answer out loud. Just notice how fast a name came.
concepts.sticker: Question box: 'What does your envy want?' (answer anonymously)
concepts.reply_fallback: Reply with what they have, not who they are.
concepts.question: If envy is a map, where is it pointing?
concepts.follow_up: Moodius take: envy is rude but useful. It points at something you want and haven't admitted. The question is whether you want their life or one thing in it.

concepts.hook: What do you pretend not to care about?
concepts.sticker: Question box
concepts.question: Why pretend?
concepts.follow_up: Moodius take: mine was being liked. I said I didn't care. I checked who'd viewed my stories. Epictetus would file that under 'not up to you' (Enchiridion 1, paraphrase).

concepts.hook: When did you last call someone for no reason?
concepts.sticker: Slider: 📞 today → 🦖 can't remember
concepts.question: Who would be glad to hear from you tonight?
concepts.follow_up: Moodius take: 'no reason' is the reason. You don't need news to ring someone.
concepts.cta: Send this to them instead of calling. Or call. Calling's better.

concepts.hook: When did you last change your mind about something important?
concepts.sticker: Slider: 🧠 this month → 🗿 never
concepts.question: What changed it: a fact, a person, or getting older?
concepts.follow_up: Moodius take: I used to think being calm meant feeling nothing. It turned out to mean feeling things without obeying all of them.

concepts.hook: Are you tired, or are you bored of something?
concepts.sticker: Poll: Tired / Bored of something
concepts.question: What would you stop if nobody minded?
concepts.follow_up: Moodius take: they feel the same on a Wednesday. Sleep fixes one of them.

concepts.hook: Your friend's business idea is bad. They ask what you think.
concepts.sticker: Poll: Honest now / Encourage, then ask questions
concepts.question: What's the kindest honest thing anyone told you?
concepts.follow_up: Moodius take: ask three good questions before you give one verdict. Marcus thought kindness only counts if it's genuine, not a performance (Meditations 11.18, paraphrase). Fake encouragement is a performance.

concepts.hook: A message makes you furious. Reply now, or tomorrow?
concepts.sticker: Poll: Now, while it's fresh / Tomorrow
concepts.question: What message are you glad you never sent?
concepts.follow_up: Seneca's top remedy for anger was delay (On Anger, paraphrase). Moodius: draft it now, send it never, decide tomorrow.
concepts.cta: Send this to the friend who replies in capitals.
concepts.source: Moodius paraphrase of Seneca, On Anger

concepts.hook: A friend needs £200. Lend it, or give it?
concepts.sticker: Poll: Lend / Give (and forget it)
concepts.question: Has money ever changed a friendship of yours?
concepts.follow_up: Polonius in Hamlet warns that a loan often loses the money and the friend (Act 1, Scene 3, paraphrase). Moodius: give only what you can forget. Lend only what you can lose.

concepts.hook: Your friend's wedding speech draft is boring. Tell them?
concepts.sticker: Poll: Tell them / Let them shine (boringly)
concepts.question: What's the line between honest and helpful?
concepts.follow_up: Moodius take: tell them about the one bit that's good and ask for more of that. Fixing beats judging.
concepts.cta: Send this to someone writing a speech.

concepts.hook: Someone cuts you off in traffic. Assume they're rude, or rushing to hospital?
concepts.sticker: Poll: Rude / Rushing
concepts.question: Which story about a stranger helps you most?
concepts.follow_up: Moodius take: you'll never know. So pick the story that ruins less of your afternoon. Marcus expected difficult people every morning, and reminded himself they were his kin (Meditations 2.1, paraphrase).

concepts.hook: What would you do this week if nobody would ever know?
concepts.sticker: Question box
concepts.question: What does that tell you about who you're doing things for?
concepts.follow_up: Moodius take: mine is read more fiction. Apparently I'm worried about being seen reading.

concepts.hook: One thing worrying you right now. Is it up to you?
concepts.sticker: Poll: Up to me / Not up to me
concepts.question: What part of it is up to you?
concepts.follow_up: Epictetus opens his handbook by splitting the world in two: what's up to us (our judgements, choices) and what isn't (other people, reputation, outcomes) (Enchiridion 1, paraphrase). Moodius: most worries are half and half. Do your half.
concepts.cta: Send this to someone carrying a worry that isn't theirs.

concepts.hook: Tonight's review: one thing you'd do differently today.
concepts.sticker: Question box
concepts.reply_fallback: Reply with one thing. No essays.
concepts.question: And one thing you did well?
concepts.follow_up: Seneca describes reviewing each day at night before sleep, without punishing himself (On Anger, Book III, paraphrase). Moodius: an evening review is a debrief, not a trial.
concepts.source: Moodius paraphrase of Seneca, On Anger, Book III

concepts.hook: Marcus started some mornings by expecting to meet difficult people. Who's your difficult person today?
concepts.sticker: Question box: describe them in 3 words (no names)
concepts.question: What do you share with them?
concepts.follow_up: Moodius paraphrase of Meditations 2.1: he expected the meddling and the ungrateful, then reminded himself they share the same nature as him. Moodius: brace for them, don't become them.

concepts.hook: One book that changed how you think. Title only.
concepts.sticker: Question box
concepts.question: What did it change?
concepts.follow_up: Follow-up shares five of your answers (question-box answers show no names) and Moodius's own pick [HIS PICK: only a book he's read].
concepts.cta: Send this to the friend who lends books and never gets them back.
concepts.format_name: Books that changed how I think

concepts.hook: A 2,000-year-old handbook starts with one idea. Guess it.
concepts.sticker: Quiz: A wake early / B some things are up to you, some aren't / C love your enemies (answer B)
concepts.question: Which one is harder to let go of: other people's opinions or outcomes?
concepts.follow_up: Epictetus, Enchiridion 1 (paraphrase). Free at Standard Ebooks. Moodius: 20 minutes to read, a lifetime to practise.
concepts.format_name: Books that changed how I think

concepts.hook: An ancient book compares the best kind of person to water. Why water?
concepts.sticker: Quiz: A it's soft / B it helps everything and doesn't compete / C it's everywhere (answer B)
concepts.question: When someone pushes, do you push back or go round?
concepts.follow_up: Tao Te Ching, chapter 8 (Legge translation, paraphrase). Authorship traditional, not certain. Moodius: water wins most arguments by not having them.
concepts.source: Tao Te Ching ch. 8, tr. Legge, Gutenberg #216
concepts.format_name: Books that changed how I think

concepts.hook: A Buddhist verse says hatred never ends by hatred. What ends it?
concepts.sticker: Question box: one word
concepts.question: What's a grudge you've set down?
concepts.follow_up: Dhammapada verse 5, tr. Müller (1881): hatred ceases by love. Modern translations say 'non-hatred'. Moodius: setting it down isn't saying it was fine.
concepts.format_name: Books that changed how I think

concepts.hook: Seneca says life isn't short. What's his point?
concepts.sticker: Slider: how much of your week is actually yours? 0 → 100%
concepts.question: Where does your week leak?
concepts.follow_up: On the Shortness of Life, chapter 1 (paraphrase): we're given enough time; we waste a lot of it. Moodius: rude, accurate, 2,000 years old.
concepts.source: Moodius paraphrase of Seneca, On the Shortness of Life, ch. 1
concepts.format_name: Books that changed how I think

concepts.hook: A stranger's kindness you still remember. Tell me in one line.
concepts.sticker: Question box
concepts.question: Did you ever get to thank them?
concepts.follow_up: Follow-up shares three answers (question-box answers show no names; never DMs without permission). Plus: people doing small kind acts underestimated how much recipients valued them.
concepts.cta: Pass one on today. Reply 'done' tomorrow.
concepts.source: Kumar & Epley, J. Experimental Psychology: General 152(1), 2023

concepts.hook: Boston, 1721. Smallpox. An enslaved man knew how to protect people. What happened next?
concepts.sticker: Quiz: A ignored / B some listened and fewer died / C he was thanked publicly (answer B)
concepts.question: Whose knowledge gets ignored because of who they are?
concepts.follow_up: Onesimus described inoculation as done in West Africa. In 1721, about 2% of inoculated people died versus about 14% who caught it naturally (figures vary by source). Inoculation was risky and is no longer used. Historical interest only.
concepts.source: HM014: Mather 1716 letter; Brown, JAMA 1988; Boylston 2012

concepts.hook: My view: you don't need closure from someone who hurt you.
concepts.sticker: Poll: Agree / Change my mind
concepts.question: What would change my mind?
concepts.follow_up: Best argument against (Moodius, steelmanned): some conversations repair things. Waiting for closure is the trap; asking once is not. Where I've landed: ask once, then stop waiting.
concepts.format_name: The argument against my own opinion

concepts.hook: My view: rest is a skill, not a reward.
concepts.sticker: Poll: Agree / Change my mind
concepts.question: What does real rest look like for you?
concepts.follow_up: Best argument against: some weeks you can't choose rest, and calling it a skill makes tired people feel they're failing. Where I've landed: a skill for when you can, never a test.
concepts.format_name: The argument against my own opinion

concepts.hook: My view: being nice and being kind are different things.
concepts.sticker: Poll: Agree / Change my mind
concepts.question: When was kind not nice?
concepts.follow_up: Best argument against: the distinction can excuse rudeness ('I'm just being honest'). Where I've landed: kind is nice with a spine, not honesty with a stick.
concepts.cta: Send this to the kindest blunt person you know.
concepts.format_name: The argument against my own opinion

concepts.hook: Vienna, 1847. A doctor asked colleagues to do one thing. Deaths fell. They mocked him. What was it?
concepts.sticker: Quiz: A wash hands / B open windows / C wear masks (answer A)
concepts.question: What good idea did you resist because of who said it?
concepts.follow_up: Ignaz Semmelweis had doctors wash their hands in chlorinated lime; deaths from childbed fever fell sharply. Many colleagues rejected it. Historical interest only.

concepts.hook: Florence Nightingale's most powerful tool in the Crimean War wasn't a lamp. What was it?
concepts.sticker: Quiz: A a chart / B a letter to the Queen / C a scalpel (answer A)
concepts.question: What would you draw a chart of, if it would change minds?
concepts.follow_up: Her diagrams showed that more soldiers died of preventable disease than of wounds, and helped push hospital reform. Moodius: a nurse who out-argued generals with a graph.
concepts.cta: Send this to someone who loves a good chart.

concepts.hook: Add Yours: a small thing that made today better.
concepts.sticker: Add Yours sticker: 'Small good thing today'
concepts.question: What's yours?
concepts.follow_up: Moodius reposts none (privacy). Just joins the chain.

concepts.hook: Add Yours: the page you'd photograph.
concepts.sticker: Add Yours sticker: 'A page worth keeping'
concepts.question: Which line?
concepts.follow_up: Moodius adds a public-domain page.

concepts.hook: You pick next week: history, mind or kindness?
concepts.sticker: Poll: History / Mind / Kindness
concepts.question: What do you want more of?
concepts.follow_up: Results shared Saturday 09:00; winner gets an extra carousel.

sequences.name: The spotlight
sequences.why: Universal embarrassment + a quiz you can get wrong + a relieving, slightly funny payoff. Tension hook, kind payoff (rule 3).

evening.title: You spilled coffee down your shirt before a meeting.
In the study, what share of the room noticed the embarrassing T-shirt?
evening.sticker: Quiz sticker: A about half / B about a quarter / C nearly everyone. Mark B correct.
evening.reply: Reply A, B or C. Answer tomorrow at 9.

morning.title: B. About a quarter.
morning.body: Students wearing an embarrassing T-shirt guessed about half the room noticed. Around a quarter did.
morning.note: Gilovich, Medvec & Savitsky, J. Personality and Social Psychology, 2000.

morning.title: The spotlight is mostly in your head.
morning.body: Which is good news, and mildly insulting.
morning.footer: Send this to the friend who still talks about the thing from 2019.

sequences.name: Up to you?
sequences.why: Epictetus arc week (12-15 Nov). Turns the oldest Stoic idea into a 2-second sort the viewer does on their own worry.

evening.title: One thing worrying you right now.
evening.body: Hold it in your head. Don't tell me what it is.

evening.title: Is it up to you?
evening.sticker: Poll sticker: Up to me / Not up to me.

morning.title: Epictetus splits the world in two.
morning.body: Up to us: our judgements and choices. Not up to us: other people, reputation, outcomes.
morning.note: Moodius paraphrase of Epictetus, Enchiridion 1. Free at Standard Ebooks.

morning.title: Most worries are half and half.
morning.body: Do your half. Put the other half down for the night.
morning.footer: Send this to someone carrying a worry that isn't theirs.

morning.title: What's the part that IS up to you?
morning.sticker: Question box: 'The part that's up to me is…'
morning.reply: Reply with one sentence. I read every one.

sequences.name: Look at the bird
sequences.why: Relationships research framed for everyone. A tiny, memorable behaviour (the 'bid') with a strong number and a sendable CTA.

evening.title: Your friend says “look at that bird”.
What do you actually do?
evening.sticker: Poll sticker: Look at the bird / Keep typing.

morning.title: It's never about the bird.
morning.body: John Gottman calls these moments 'bids'. Couples still together six years after his newlywed study had turned toward bids 86% of the time. Couples who divorced: 33%.
morning.note: The Gottman Institute. Lab finding reported in his books, not a journal paper. Works for friendships too.

morning.title: Look at the bird.
morning.body: Then finish the message. It'll wait. The person might not.
morning.footer: Send this to the person who always shows you birds.

sequences.name: Calm down or get excited
sequences.why: Practical, counter-intuitive, tested. People choose 'calm' and are surprised; the payoff is a tool they can use tomorrow.

evening.title: Heart racing. Big moment in five minutes.
Which works better?
evening.sticker: Poll sticker: Calm down / I'm excited.

morning.title: “I'm excited” won.
morning.body: People told to say “I am excited” before singing or speaking in public did better than people told to say “I am calm”.

morning.title: You can't always calm down. You can rename it.
morning.body: Same racing heart. Different story about it.
morning.footer: Send this to someone with a big day this week.

morning.title: What's the scary thing on your calendar?
morning.sticker: Question box: 'This week I'm nervous about…'
morning.reply: Reply with one word. I'll be rooting for you.

sequences.name: Closure (argued against)
sequences.why: The 'argument against my own opinion' format: Moodius takes a stance, steelmans the other side and invites disagreement. Builds trust and long replies.

evening.kicker: The argument against my own opinion
evening.title: You don't need closure from someone who hurt you.
evening.body: Waiting for an apology can keep you tied to them for years.
evening.note: Some conversations really do repair things. Refusing to ask can be its own kind of pride.

evening.title: Who wins?
evening.sticker: Poll sticker: Your view / The case against.

evening.title: What would change my mind?
evening.reply: Reply and argue with me. Politely.

morning.title: Ask once. Then stop waiting.
morning.body: Asking isn't the trap. Waiting is. Thank you to everyone who argued with me.
morning.footer: Tonight: one you'll disagree with even more.

sequences.name: A stranger's kindness
sequences.why: Positive, shareable, collects real stories (question-box answers show no names). Backed by a 2023 kindness study.

evening.title: Someone you'll never see again did something you still remember.
What did they do?
evening.reply: Reply with one line. I'll share a few (no names).

morning.title: [Share 3 question-box answers here, by hand.]
morning.body: Question-box answers show no names. Never share a DM without asking first.
morning.note: Hand-posted frame. In the scheduled version, use the frame below instead.

morning.title: Small kindness lands bigger than you think.
morning.body: People who did a small kind act for a stranger underestimated how much it meant to them.
morning.note: Kumar & Epley, J. Experimental Psychology: General, 2023.

morning.title: Pass one on today.
morning.body: Reply 'done' tomorrow. No details needed.

sequences.name: Vienna, 1847
sequences.why: Forgotten history with a gasp-level answer and a moral about ego, not about the past. Awe/surprise travel (Berger & Milkman).

evening.title: Vienna, 1847. A doctor asked colleagues to do one thing.
What did he ask them to do?
evening.sticker: Quiz sticker: A wash their hands / B open the windows / C wear masks. Mark A correct.
evening.reply: Reply A, B or C. Answer at 9.

morning.title: A. Wash their hands.
morning.body: Ignaz Semmelweis had doctors wash in chlorinated lime. Deaths from childbed fever fell sharply. Many colleagues rejected it anyway.
morning.note: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Ignaz Semmelweis'. History, not medical advice.

morning.title: What good idea did you resist because of who said it?
morning.reply: Reply with one word. Mine: going to bed earlier.

sequences.name: The awe walk
sequences.why: Living Body without fitness clichés: a free, 15-minute practice with a delightful detail (the selfies shrank).

evening.title: Older adults took one 15-minute 'awe walk' a week for 8 weeks.
evening.body: Something odd happened to their photos.

evening.title: What changed?
evening.sticker: Quiz sticker: A more selfies / B they got smaller in the frame / C nothing. Mark B correct.
evening.reply: Reply A, B or C. Answer at 9.
options: they got smaller in the frame

morning.title: B. More sky, less self.
morning.body: Awe walkers also reported more joy and warmer feelings toward others than people on ordinary walks.
morning.note: Sturm et al., Emotion, 2022. Small study.
options: they got smaller in the frame

morning.title: When did something last make you feel small, in a good way?

morning.reply: Reply with a number from 1 to 10.

morning.title: Fifteen minutes. No podcast.
morning.body: Look up more than you look down.
morning.footer: Send this to someone who needs a walk.

morning.title: Honest vs encouraging.
morning.body: Saves them money and months.
morning.note: They may need to find it out themselves, and keep you as a friend.

morning.title: Ask three good questions before one verdict.
morning.body: Marcus thought kindness only counts when it's genuine, not a performance. Fake encouragement is a performance. (Meditations 11.18, paraphrase)

morning.title: The kindest honest thing anyone ever told you?

sequences.name: The 21-day myth
sequences.why: 'Myth or replicated': flatters curiosity, corrects a famous number with a real one, and comforts people who are struggling with a habit.

evening.title: “A new habit takes 21 days.”
evening.body: You've heard it. Is it true?

evening.title: In the study, the typical time to automatic was…
evening.sticker: Quiz sticker: A 21 days / B about 66 days / C 254 days. Mark B correct.
evening.reply: Reply A, B or C. Answer at 9.

morning.title: B. About 66 days.
morning.body: The middle of the range. It took some people 18 days and others 254.
morning.note: Lally et al., European J. Social Psychology, 2010.

morning.title: If it's day 22 and still feels like work…
morning.body: …you're not broken. You're average. Keep going.
morning.footer: Send this to someone on day 22.

morning.title: What habit are you on day 'some' of?
morning.sticker: Emoji slider 🐢 → 🚀: 'How automatic is it yet?'
morning.reply: Reply with the habit, one word.

sequences.name: Envy as a map
sequences.why: 'An uncomfortable question' done gently: private reflection first, then a reframe that makes an ugly feeling useful.

evening.title: Who do you envy?
evening.body: Don't answer. Just notice how fast a name came.

evening.title: What do they have that you want?
evening.sticker: Question box: 'What does your envy want?' (answers show no names)
evening.reply: Reply with the thing, not the person.

morning.title: Envy is rude but useful.
morning.body: It points at something you want and haven't admitted yet.

morning.title: Do you want their life, or one thing in it?
morning.sticker: Poll sticker: Their life / One thing in it.

sequences.name: The note you keep not writing
sequences.why: Gratitude with a twist (people underestimate the impact). Ends in an action, measured by a one-word 'sent' reply.

evening.title: You write someone a thank-you note.
evening.body: How happy will they be, really?

evening.title: Compared with your guess, they'll be…
evening.sticker: Quiz sticker: A a bit happy / B as you'd guess / C happier than you'd guess. Mark C correct.
evening.reply: Reply A, B or C. Answer at 9.

morning.title: C. Happier than you'd guess.
morning.body: Writers of gratitude letters underestimated how surprised and happy recipients would feel, and overestimated the awkwardness.

morning.title: Who has done more for you than you've told them?
morning.sticker: Question box: first name only, or just 'got one'
morning.reply: Reply with a first name. That's your note.

morning.title: Three lines is enough.
morning.body: What they did. What it changed. Thank you.

sequences.name: Nightingale's chart
sequences.why: Overturns a cliché (the lamp) with a nerdy, empowering fact. Shareable to 'the friend who loves a chart'.

evening.title: Florence Nightingale's most powerful tool wasn't a lamp.
Her secret weapon:
evening.sticker: Quiz sticker: A a chart / B a letter to the Queen / C a scalpel. Mark A correct.
evening.reply: Reply A, B or C. Answer at 9.

morning.title: A. A chart.
morning.body: Her diagrams showed more soldiers in the Crimean War died of preventable disease than of wounds, and helped push hospital reform.

morning.title: A nurse out-argued generals with a graph.
morning.body: Kindness sometimes looks like homework.
morning.footer: Send this to someone who loves a good chart.

sequences.name: 120 minutes
sequences.why: A slider people answer honestly, a concrete number to aim for, and a soft, non-preachy nudge outside. Weekend slot.

evening.title: Minutes outside this week.
evening.body: Real outside. The car park doesn't count.

evening.title: How many?
evening.sticker: Emoji slider 🏢 → 🌳: 'Minutes in nature this week'
evening.reply: Reply with your guess in minutes.

morning.title: The number in one big survey: 120.
morning.body: Among about 20,000 people in England, those who spent at least 120 minutes a week in nature were more likely to report good health and wellbeing.
morning.note: White et al., Scientific Reports, 2019. Linked, not proven to cause it.

morning.title: That's 17 minutes a day.
morning.body: A park bench counts. So does a tree you walk past slowly.
morning.footer: Send this to the friend who'd come with you.
